To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the expression of host fluorescent protein pigments in corals can promote coral adaptation to deeper-water light conditions by transforming blue light into orange–red light.

(1) fluorescent proteins in coral hosts transform the light environment to promote the functioning of symbiotic algae, (2) this mechanism is important in deep-water coral reefs, and (3) it is a previously unreported mechanism of adaptation/acclimatiza-tion to the light environment.

fluorescent protein pigments in corals can transform the prevalent blue light to orange-red light, and that this facilitates a more uniform distribution of light across symbiont cells in the host, which promotes the functioning of the holobiont in deeper reefs.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms by which corals can adapt to the low light intensity and reduced spectral quality of deeper reefs.
the mechanisms used by reef-building corals to respond to the extreme light environments encountered in deeper reefs.
the ecological significance of the photoconvertible red fluorescence protein in the coral holobions.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the depth distribution of reef building corals exposes their symbiotic dinoflagellates, Symbiodinium, to extreme gradients in light intensity and spectral quality.
the presence of pcRFP is a mechanism that promotes coral adaptation to deeper reefs by increasing the penetration of light into the tissues and enhancing the photosynthesis of Symbiodinium.
fluorescent proteins are a mechanism for coral acclimatization to low light conditions in mesophotic reefs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the light environment is a major driver for the structure and functioning of coral reefs.

corals can use host pigments to transform blue light into orange and red light, which can then penetrate deeper within the zooxanthellate tissue, facilitating a more homogeneous distribution and absorption of photons by the zooxanthella community.
fluorescent proteins can be used to transform light in the holobiont, which may be a mechanism for adaptation to the deep reef.
The main takeaway from our work is that
host pigments can be an important mechanism to support the function of the coral– Symbiodinium association under low-light and reduced spectral quality conditions.
the light environment experienced by corals is more complex than previously assumed.

the coral holobionic system is capable of adapting and/or acclimatizing to low light environments through the expression of fluorescent proteins that transform the light environment to one that is more suitable for the functioning of the symbiotic association.
